summary: The English of Genesis 1:6–13 is accurate and follows the Hebrew closely; no reading-line change is needed. The faults are in the apparatus: Rashi's reading of יְהִי רָקִיעַ ('let the expanse become firm') was wrongly set aside as not applicable, the sense of יְהִי in 1:6 and of פְּרִי in 1:11–12 were mis-assigned, and two accent notes (1:7, 1:10) misplace or misdescribe the accents. Two Rashi summaries are inaccurate (the laaz in 1:11, the קַל וָחֹמֶר in 1:12), and the 1:11 note credits Ibn Ezra with Rashi's דשא/עשב distinction.

patches.reason: The jussive יְהִי of a creative command is 'come into being' (BDB Qal II), not 'exist, be in existence' (Qal III.1).

value.summary: Rashi: יְהִי רָקִיעַ means 'let the expanse become firm' (יֶחֱזַק הָרָקִיעַ): the heavens made on day one were still moist (לַחִים) and set hard on the second day at God's rebuke, as Job 26:11 says the pillars of heaven tremble and are astonished at His rebuke. On this reading the verb strengthens an existing heaven; the English 'let there be' follows the plain sense of a new making (cf. Ibn Ezra), and Rashi's reading is kept here.

patches.reason: Rashi's comment is a reading of the words יְהִי רָקִיעַ (not a homily): it makes the verb 'become firm', not 'come to be'. It bears on the plain sense, so the English, which does not adopt it, must record it, not mark it not-applicable.

The English 'expanse' (something stretched out) adopts Ibn Ezra's sense of רָקִיעַ, as the translator's own note says; only his identification with the air is left open. 'follows' fits better than 'records'.

patches.value: מִתַּחַת לְ is a compound preposition, 'below, beneath'; the לְ introduces what the waters are below
patches.reason: The לְ here is part of the compound preposition מִתַּחַת לְ, not a לְ of possession ('of, belonging to').

value: The wayyiqtol וַיַּעַשׂ continues the narrative of the command; עשה here is 'set in order, finish' (Rashi, Ramban).
בֵּין ... וּבֵין is the second way the idiom is built; Ibn Ezra lists the three forms.
מֵעַל לָרָקִיעַ means 'above' with space between, not 'on' the expanse.
The zinor on אֱלֹהִים and the segol on הָרָקִיעַ set the making apart from the dividing; the silluq closes the verse after וַיְהִי־כֵן.
patches.reason: The zinor stands on אֱלֹהִים֮ (1:7.2), not on הָרָקִיעַ, which carries the segol.
The gloss should give the sense used in the English line, which names it 'Sky' (and 1:9 'the sky'); 'heavens' stays in the literal line.

value: The object (the gathering of the waters) is placed before the verb, so the perfect קָרָא is used.
יַמִּים is the plural: the one gathering is named by several seas.
כִּי־טוֹב: a clause of seeing, 'that it was good'.
The paseq after אֱלֹהִים and the pashta on לַיַּבָּשָׁה lead to the zaqef on אֶרֶץ, which divides the two namings; the etnaḥta on יַמִּים sets the namings apart from God's seeing.
patches.reason: The qadma on וַיִּקְרָא is a conjunctive accent and divides nothing; the namings are divided by the zaqef on אֶרֶץ, with the etnaḥta on יַמִּים.
Fruit of a tree is BDB sense 1 (fruit, of ground and of trees, Gn 1:11–12); sense 3 is the figurative fruit (result) of conduct.

patches.value: 'Green growth' for דֶּשֶׁא follows Rashi: דשא is the earth's green covering, עשב the individual plants (Ramban disputes this and takes דשא as the young growth). Ibn Ezra glosses only the verb: תַּדְשֵׁא is תַּצְמִיחַ. 'Fruit trees' keeps עֵץ פְּרִי; Rashi's reading of a tree that tastes of fruit is kept in the commentary.
patches.reason: Ibn Ezra does not make the דשא/עשב distinction; he says only that תדשא means תצמיח. The distinction is Rashi's.

patches.value: Rashi: תַּדְשֵׁא הָאָרֶץ means the earth should fill and cover itself with a garment of plants. In Old French דֶּשֶׁא is ארבריץ ('herbage'), all kinds mixed together, while each root by itself is called עֵשֶׂב. The English 'sprout green growth'.
patches.reason: Rashi's laaz ארבריץ is Old French for 'herbage', not 'arbres' (trees); the summary also omitted his point that each root by itself is עשב.
Fruit of a tree is BDB sense 1; sense 3 is figurative.

patches.value: Rashi: although לְמִינֵהוּ was not said of the grasses in their command, they heard that the trees were so commanded and reasoned a fortiori (קַל וָחֹמֶר) for themselves, as the aggadah in Ḥullin explains. The English gives each group 'of its own kind'.
patches.reason: נָשְׂאוּ קַ"וָ בְּעַצְמָן means they drew an a fortiori inference for themselves, not that they 'carried it on themselves'.

verdicts.comment: Rashi reads 'let the expanse become firm'; the English 'let there be' keeps the plain sense of a new thing made, in line with Ibn Ezra (the expanse formed as the air). Rashi and Ibn Ezra differ, so the English may choose; Rashi is now recorded.
'made' read as 'set it in its place'.
He joins וַיְהִי־כֵן to 1:8; the English keeps it with 1:7 by the accents (silluq), and Rashi does not support the join. Recorded.
An etymology of שָׁמַיִם; it does not change the English.
He reads 1:9 as a pluperfect ('had said'); the English keeps the sequence of days, which Rashi 1:7 (the work of the waters begun on day two and finished on day three) supports. Recorded.
Rashi's 'tree whose wood tastes like its fruit' is a midrashic reading; the plain 'fruit trees' stands and Ibn Ezra offers no contrary plain sense. Recorded.
The pack's text is a single letter.
